To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the best procedure for inducing word meanings is to compute a point-wise product of a word's context vector with its target vector, (b) this procedure is robust across a variety of evaluation measures, (c) the procedure is robust to the number of training examples, and (d) the best evaluation measure is the cosine of the angle between the target and induced vectors.

(1) the best procedure for representing word meanings from word frequencies in a text is the standard vector model, (2) the best way to validate these representations is to measure their similarity to the representations of human participants, and (3) the best way of doing this is to measure the correlation between the similarity of pairs of words in the vector model, and the similarity of pairs as rated by humans.

(1) the best way of representing word meaning from co-occurrence data involves using the co-occurrence counts themselves, not their log-transforms, and using the cosine similarity metric, not Euclidean similarity, (2) the best way to evaluate the resulting representations involves using the cosine similarity measure and a test based on random permutations of the data, and (3) the best way for a human to interpret the resulting representations is to treat them as similarity measures.
